chapter: Brass bands and the ERA/WPA band
title: ERA band concerts at Jackson Square and public performances
summary: The ERA band played weekend concerts, rehearsed at Patona, and split into groups for schools, parks and institutions.

story.theme_name: Making a living: hard times, day jobs and scarce work
story.community_name: The Depression years and the WPA band

blocks.x: They would all play together, all those musicians at one time?
All those fellas would play together at one time. They had parts.
Boy, that was quite a loud band, wasn't it?

Well, they would cut them down, I'll tell you. And when this picture was taken out in the park at that time, they must have given us, some fella from New York must have given us $75 or something like that. They liked the band, but they would cut you down. And he would make you play and he would cut you down, but he wouldn't last. But he'd make you make them introductions, and if it was double 40, come back to my 40, and then .
How long had you made this picture in Jackson Park? Were you playing for this fellow?
Well, we would go out there and have concepts.
You had regular concepts there in Jackson?
Yeah, concepts in the Jackson Square. That's where this picture we took, we had concepts out there.
On the weekends. And we were at the Fifth Ward Artilette Club at that time. Patona.
Yeah, that's where we used to have our band rights at Patona. And we'd come out there and have our concert.
You didn't rehearse parts in there, only a couple blocks.

That's right. Then we'd begin having projects, taking it from different parts. Sometimes we'd go to different schools, Shakespeare Park, and sometimes we'd go to the jailhouse, go to the municipal boy home, and then we'd begin to go everywhere with these concerts.
Did the whole band go, or just a small group?

Well, the whole band, then we would split them up. Sometimes the school wanted groups, then they'd split us up in groups. And we'd go out in groups and play for different schools all around like that. There's something like this Roe of War I. You want music, well, for certain cases, there wasn't no money being made at it, just a public performance, you know? So they would split us up and then we'd make our budget like that. In fact, every school we would go. Yeah. Yeah. And go out and play for the prisoners even now. Yeah.
